utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Will the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-98-34-PT, the Prosecutor versus Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I'd like to welcome all the participants to this Status Conference; the lawyers, Mr. Martinovic, the Registry staff, the translators, and anyone else who is helping to make it possible. The first thing on the agenda is I would like the counsel for the parties, the Prosecution and for Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Martinovic, to announce their appearances. First the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, Madam President. The Prosecutor is represented by Mr. Douglas Stringer, on my right-hand side, and Mr. Manuel Bouwknecht, our case manager, together with myself Franck Terrier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let's have the counsel for Mr. Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone present, in particular to you, Your Honour. My name is Kresimir Krsnik, and I'm the Defence counsel for Mr. Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Martinovic's counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I would also like to greet my learned colleagues from the Prosecution. My name is Branko Seric and I'm the Defence counsel for Vinko Martinovic. I'm a member of the Croatian Bar Association. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Welcome. Now, my understanding is that Mr. Naletilic will not be with us because he is not feeling up to it, and he has sent a note for the record indicating that he wishes you to represent him and for the Status Conference to go ahead. Is that correct, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct, Your Honour. This morning when I visited my client, he felt -- he was very ill, he was medicated, and he expressed his doubts as to whether he would be able to be here at the Status Conference. That is in keeping with what the Defence counsel has been saying right from the beginning, from the first Status Conference, and that is that we need an expert medical examination of my client. This is under way even as we speak, and then well have more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krsnik. You are right. Of course the Chamber has ordered that such an examination to take place. The report will be given to us on May 25th, at which time we will be in a better position to evaluate your client's ability to undertake the trial. But we are sure that you will represent him with skill and ardour in the meantime. The Status Conference, which, as you all know, is mandated within 120 days after the Initial Appearance, and 120 days thereafter, under Rule 65 bis, very briefly, it has three objectives which I will remind you of. I know it's very warm in this courtroom, and I hope that we'll be able to achieve all of these objectives and be out of here hopefully within an hour to an hour and a half. The first is to facilitate the exchange of information between the two parties and to examine the progress of the case to make sure that there are no undue delays. In that regard, we're going to discuss very briefly the disclosure of information that's required under the Tribunal's Rules 66, 67, 68, 94 bis, and 94 ter. The second objective of the conference is to manage the preparation by both sides so that the trial will be as efficient as possible. This includes various procedures that may speed the trial up, such as parties agreements on undisputed facts, judicial notice, affidavits, and perhaps depositions. It also includes the pre-trial filings that are required under Rule 65 ter. The third is to give the accused, in this case Mr. Martinovic, at the end of the proceeding, a chance to tell us any concerns he has regarding the conditions of detention. Right off the bat we'll move toward the first of those requirements. So I will ask both sides where you are presently on the status of pre-trial disclosures. Now, I would remind you that at Mr. Naletilic's Initial Appearance, the Prosecutor indicated that the supporting materials that are required to be given to the accused, to the Defence, under Rule 66(A)(i) would be disclosed promptly. I would now ask the Prosecution what has happened, has that been done; that is, the disclosures that are required under Rule 66(A)(i).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, as regards the obligations of the Prosecutor to disclose supporting material, this measure has been fulfilled by the Prosecutor as regards both of the accused. Concerning Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Krsnik, this was done, as we indicated to the Tribunal, at the day of the Initial Appearance of Mr. Naletilic, that is, on the 24th of March. We are now fulfilling our obligation in application of Rule 66(A)(i). As regards Mr. Martinovic and his counsel, Mr. Seric, we have already disclosed on several occasions 191 witness statements involving 134 witnesses. Some of the witnesses had given several statements. These statements have been given to Mr. Seric, who is representing Mr. Martinovic. As regards Mr. Naletilic and his counsel, Mr. Krsnik, we are now able to disclose these same statements, because we have disclosed to both of the accused all of the statements that are available to us even if they concern the other accused primarily, so we are now able to disclose to Mr. Krsnik, for the accused Mr. Naletilic, these statements as well. This leaves us with about 40 statements that still have to be disclosed. We cannot do it today in the Serbo-Croatian language because we have some problems, involving the translation problems this Tribunal is familiar with. Additional resources are being mobilised, and we have asked for a new deadline to be indicated for the disclosure in the Serbo-Croatian language. We now are able to disclose the statements in the English language but we don't know whether this will be sufficient for the counsel. At the end of next month, we will have all of the remaining statements, including those in the language of the accused, and we will be able to disclose them at that time to both Mr. Seric and Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me make sure I understand you, Mr. Terrier. When you're talking about the witness statements, the 40 statements that you have not yet been able to translate into the language of the accused, are those witness statements under 66(A)(ii)? In other words, those are statements of witnesses that the Prosecutor intends to call to testify at trial? You have already disclosed the supporting material under 66(A)(i); is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is absolutely correct, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You are saying, if I understand you, that you need until the end of next month, that would be the end of June, to finish with the 40 statements. Did I understand you correctly that that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you have, Madam President. The translation service needs that time in order to finish its work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Let me now ask the Defence counsel, first Mr. Krsnik, whether or not you have received the supporting materials, you have received many of the witness statements except for the 40 that the Prosecutor referred to. In other words, is the information he has given us in accord with what you have received, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So far I have received statements of about 30 witnesses, that was at the Initial Appearance, and I haven't received anything else until this day. If I understood him correctly, I will get today the statements of an additional 190 witnesses. Because right now the Defence counsel for Mr. Naletilic has about 30 witness statements so far, that's the only thing that has been disclosed to us by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, Mr. Krsnik has received, as I have said, the documents that were presented to the Confirming Judge. So that was pursuant to Rule 66(A)(i). What is still pending and what we still have to do in order to fulfil our obligations are a number of other documents. As regards these other documents, we are able to disclose them shortly -- not today, because we have problems involving copying and so on -- we will be able very soon to disclose to Mr. Krsnik the documents that have already been disclosed to Mr. Seric, that is, 191 statements, witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Those 191 do not include the 40 that you need a longer period of time for; is that right? But those 191, when you say "in a little while," I take that to mean that within the next week or two you will get those, except for the 40, to Mr. Krsnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me ask you one further question, Mr. Krsnik. The fact that Mr. Terrier says he needs until the end of next month for these -- assume you get the 190 in a week or so. He needs some additional time, I think a month and a half, for the additional 40 to be translated into Serbo-Croat. Is that satisfactory to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is acceptable to me because I have no other option. Your Honour, on my own initiative, three weeks ago, I got in touch with my colleagues for the Prosecution, asking them when I will receive the other witness statements. So I did that on my own initiative, and I have nothing else to say. I have to be happy with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me speak now with Mr. Seric and make sure that he agrees with the information that Mr. Terrier has given us about the receipt of both the supporting materials and the 191 witness documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the information provided by my learned colleague from the Prosecution is correct. I did receive the 132 witness statements, and the Defence counsel for Mr. Martinovic is aware of that, is in receipt of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. I think we have that in hand. My last question on the 66 situation is there is, I take it, no possibility that the translations can be -- of the remaining 40 statements can be accomplished sooner than a month and a half. In the meantime, however, you can provide them in the English language; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, the statements are in English. They were taken in the English language. We can disclose them in English if my learned colleagues wish so. But we cannot force the Translation Service of this Tribunal to work faster than they do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me ask the two counsel for the Defence. Will it be of any assistance to you to get them in English ahead of the time that they come to you in Serbo-Croat or not? Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being and at this stage of the proceedings, I don't think it would be of any assistance to me if I were to receive those witness statements in English. But I would just like to make a note. I don't want to meddle in the job of my colleagues, but I believe that those witnesses are all from the former Yugoslavia, and I'm surprised that they do not give statements in their native language. So it seems that their original statements are being translated into English and then have to be translated back into Serbo-Croat. So I just have this little remark. That's rather odd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Seric, do you want them in English, or are you happy to wait? Not happy, but reconciled to wait until ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, it will not change my situation to a considerable degree if I receive these statements in English, precisely because the Defence team, once they receive the statements in English, we can understand them, but we have to involve our client in the defence, in the preparation of the defence, and that really limits our possibility to do so if we don't have those statements in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. I understand your position. Mr. Terrier, I would request of you that you and your team keep on top of this, and if there is any likelihood that the translation will be delayed beyond the period that you are now estimating for me that you will be in touch with me as the Pre-Trial Judge to let me know if there is any possibility that they will not be able to make that deadline. As you know, the advanced disclosure of witness statements is very important, and unless it's done, it can cause very untoward delays later on in the proceedings. I know you're aware of that. At this point, I would also remind the Prosecution of their duty to disclose any exculpatory evidence under Rule 68 as they move along. That means that any evidence that they come upon which, in the terms of the Rule, tends to suggests the innocence or to mitigate the guilt of the accused, or to affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence, and I'm sure you're aware of that and you'll keep on top of that. Okay. The next question I would ask is to the Defence lawyers: Whether or not they intend, under Rule 66(B), to make a request to review the Prosecution's exhibits. If they do, I know that they are aware that under Rule 67(C), I believe it is, that the Defence -- that the Prosecutor, in turn, will be entitled to inspect any exhibits, books, documents, et cetera, which the Defence has. Do either or both of the Defence lawyers intend to invoke 66(B) for reciprocal disclosure, reciprocal discovery of the documents? Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: How about you, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just like my colleague; for the time being, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. It does speed things up sometimes, if you will. So you might think hard about that as you proceed through your preparation of the case. I'm also reminding you that under Rule 94 bis, any expert reports must be disclosed, the Rule says, as early as possible. And within 14 days after any such report is submitted to the Trial Chamber, the parties must say whether they accept the report or wish to cross-examine it. My question, and I'll start with the Prosecution, would be, at this point, whether or not the Prosecution thinks there will be expert reports that they will be tendering to the Chambers, and if so, approximately when?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, for the time being we do not think we will invoke more than one expert report by Mr. Colin Kaiser, who is an expert from UNESCO, and he deals with religious and cultural institutions. This particular issue was quite important throughout Bosnia and Mostar, and he made a list of damage caused to these institutions in that area. It is quite a voluminous report. So far we've only had it in the English language, but it concerns the area of Bosnia in its entirety, not only the area of Mostar. So we think, for the time being, that we will be using this report, because it is in connection with paragraph 11 of the indictment, where the Prosecutor states that the destruction of religious and cultural objects was done, was made. I'm referring to paragraph 11 of the indictment. I should like to ask a question at this moment, and it concerns our obligation to translate this report. The report is in the English language. Do we have to translate it -- do we have to translate it in its entirety, or only the passages, the relevant passages which concern the area of Herzegovina, and the area of Mostar in particular?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm consulting the Rule for the moment. The Rule certainly doesn't say anything about it having to be translated in the language of the accused, but since I am relatively new at this business, let me at least preliminarily consult Mr. Fourmy, who has had somewhat more experience along these lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: To answer your question, at this juncture, it doesn't appear to me that the report itself is required by the Rule to be translated in that language. Now, of course if an expert comes on, or if the expert comes on, then the expert would be subject to the expert witness rule. However, I would think that if it were possible, that if there were key provisions of the report, it would facilitate matters greatly if there were a translation of that. But that's certainly my preliminary feeling about this. However, if upon doing any further research I come to a different conclusion, I will let both parties be aware of that. When do you think that you would be submitting such a report either to the Defence, for their advance knowledge, or later on to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, I can just inform you about my experience in another case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even, of course, in the Rules, and I'm referring in particular to Rule 67, the Rule does not oblige us to have that translation. But we have a similar obligation in some other systems. What concerns me is the following: I think it is perfectly normal, logical, and feasible, without too much difficult, to translate the pages that concern the area of Mostar and Herzegovina, but it is absolutely useless, on the other hand, and it would be a waste of time, if we have to translate the report in its entirety. The report consists of about 400 pages and it concerns the area of Bosnia as a whole, and some areas in Croatia, in particular, the area of Dubrovnik. So what we would like to do is that we be allowed not to translate the entire report but only, and as soon as it is practically possible, the pages that concern the area of Mostar, and, I think, I'm not quite sure, that it must be about 50 pages, 50 pages concerning the area of Mostar, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me get the reaction of Mr. Seric and Mr. Krsnik. Would that be satisfactory to you, if the parts of the report which have any relevance to the episodes that we're considering in this case are translated to you in the native language? Will that be satisfactory to you? Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems logical to the Defence that the Prosecutors should stick to their indictment and to translate only those parts that are relevant for the indictment, which would enable us to defend our clients to the best of our abilities. I do not see any sense in translating things that concern the overall situation in Bosnia, in particular in Croatia, because these proceedings have to do with the indictment that was issued by our learned colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Fine. Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as regards the destruction in Bosnia and in the wider area, my client, Vinko Martinovic, doesn't have anything to do with that. Only the things that happened in Mostar have to do with him, and he knows best what happened there. So we agree -- I agree that only those parts that are relevant for this area be translated, and then we can examine it and challenge those parts that we deem fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. I'm also informed, and you can correct me if I'm mistaken here, Mr. Terrier, that the author of the report, Mr. Kaiser, is it, has already testified before this Tribunal in another case. So there will be available transcripts which have been translated in B/C/S as to his testimony. Okay. Now, I'd like then -- and do you have a rough idea when you're likely to submit that report? If the conditions which you specified and which are satisfactory to the Defence; namely, just the translation of the relevant portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, frankly speaking, today I am unable to give you a specific date. We have to contact the Translation Service once again for that purpose. And I do not think that we would be able to disclose a translation of those 50 pages before the month of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I have in mind, although it is skipping ahead some, that we would have another Pre-Trial Conference in which I hope many of these things will have settled into, probably in early July. That would satisfy both the 120-day period for your client, Mr. Krsnik, and allow some of these matters, including the witness statements that you talked about, to be settled in. So that timing sounds as though it's a reasonable one. Let me move on to a quick survey of whether or not the parties have considered -- I hope they have -- and will continue to consider and perhaps to execute some of the methods for shortening trial. Now, the first obvious method would be taking some of the testimony by deposition, pursuant to 71, or even possibly by video conference, to 71 bis. Does the Prosecution presently have any intention to take any of the testimony by deposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam President. When we established, initially, contact with Defence counsel and when we were able to assess these points of agreement and disagreement, so once we establish that kind of contact, we will be able to tell you what witnesses exactly can be heard here by the full Chamber and what witnesses can be heard, in accordance with Rule 71, by videolink, if, of course, it involves certain problems, in particular those relating to security. So we should like to ask the Chamber to use this particular provision for a limited number -- a certain number of witnesses, but today we are not able to provide you with that list because we have to establish this type of contact with our colleagues from the Defence so that we can see on what issues we can agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that, and I assume again that by the time -- if we have another Pre-Trial Conference, say, in early July, you will be far enough long to be able to inform us. How about the Defence? Mr. Krsnik and then Mr. Seric. Do you have any intention of using deposition testimony for any of your witnesses? Go ahead, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence does not intend to do so, in particular as the Defence counsel for Mr. Naletilic thinks that this Court is a court of the highest standard. The Defence does not wish to discuss these proceedings in terms of expediting them or making them shorter. We want to see the justice done and to be done in its entirety. For that to be done, we think that all the witnesses have to come here, be heard before this Trial Chamber, and cross-examined, because we already have some information about the conditions -- circumstances in which the witness statements were taken in Bosnia. We know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sure that -- I'm sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to complete my sentence. So in principle, the stand of the Defence is that all the witnesses have to come here and be heard before this Trial Chamber and be cross-examined here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand your position, though I'm sure you're aware that if testimony is taken by deposition, that means that it is taken subject to cross-examination. And indeed, sometimes justice best done by being done as quickly as is possible under fairness. But how about you, Mr. Seric? Have you considered the possibility of depositions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to support the statement of my colleague, Mr. Krsnik, but I wish to give a theoretical introduction on which we base our view. I will repeat that this International Criminal Tribunal was established by the Security Council of the United Nations to prosecute serious violations of humanitarian law in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. It's an authority par excellence for the whole world and for Croatia. That is why we, the Defence, deem that we should pursue the principle of adversarial proceedings and direct examination, and in the interests of justice and of having a fair trial to which we are obliged under Article 20 of the Statute, the witnesses have to be heard before the Trial Chamber. The Defence wishes to stress that our experience so far tells us something about how the witnesses feel when they testify at home, so to speak, because it may, and indeed it happened already, that it may be different than when they testify before the Court. And it is precisely this feeling, this sense, that they are testifying in their own home, in their own village, in their own environment, and that after they inculpate my client very seriously, they just cross the street and go back to their home as if nothing has happened, without even seeing the accused, and the entire street, the entire village, knows that they testified the way they did. And then at the same time, somebody else who has an impact -- who affects their financial and other status, and that has happened, the Defence has information that in some cases the witnesses' houses were not repaired until they testified, so they have this feeling that their testimony affects the quality of their lives, and indeed their security, this affects the accuracy of their testimony. Well, we are all experts here. We know what Grasburger [phoen] wrote about this issue. The effect of the environment from which the witnesses come is not so strong. If they are there, they have to testify the way that the environment expects them too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I think I understand your position and the reasons why you're taking it. At this point, I would simply remind you that the Rules of the Tribunal do provide for depositions to be taken where it is in the interests of justice to do so. Now, if you decide you do not want to do any of your witnesses by deposition, you have given us some of the reasons to do so. If the Prosecution, however, decides that it wishes to advance some of its witness testimony by deposition, I'm sure there will be an opportunity for you to object. But I would again remind you that many of the trials before the Tribunal have had deposition testimony in them, which, I think it is the consensus, they have not suffered to any degree for lack of fairness. And in some cases, it is a question not of getting the absolute best possible means in every case but of losing the witness altogether if the witness cannot come by deposition. But I don't think we have to, at this juncture, go into all of the arguments, pro and con, on that. I wished merely to find out your intent on these. The same is true of the next two questions which I may surmise you may answer similarly, but you may surprise me, and I'll ask the Prosecution first whether or not they've identified any facts that they think might be the subject of judicial notice, pursuant to Rule 94. In some of the cases that we've had, there have been consensual -- consent of both sides to recognising some adjudicated facts. Now, I'm not sure that there are that many similar proceedings to the issues that are involved in this case, but I wonder if you've thought about. If not, if you will think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, I will reply to your question as completely as possible. Will you just help me to understand, and to add something under Rule 71, the way we understand it at the Office of the Prosecutor. Let me first tell you, and I should like to answer the argument of Mr. Seric, namely, that some of the witnesses could be led to testify in a different manner. My answer is that Rule 71 does not provide that it can be heard in their kitchen at home. This is something that's transmitted here, to this courtroom. In those conditions and bearing in mind those circumstances, I have to say that the witnesses will be in an appropriate environment and they will have to testify sincerely and as completely as possible. Let me add one more thing. The witnesses who will be saying, maybe, "I recognise the accused Naletilic or the accused Martinovic," those witnesses, the witnesses who are able to identify the accused and to say that the accused committed a crime, namely, the fact witnesses, I think that those witnesses will have to be called and testify before the Chamber. This will not be the case of all of the witnesses that we intend to call. Other witnesses will bring other important information to this Chamber but they will not necessarily identify either of the accused. And those witnesses are the ones that I had in mind when I said that they could be heard if not by the procedure provided -- that they could be heard by the use of videolink. So this is my answer to the position exposed by my learned colleagues. If we have a fact witness, that witness is -- of course, it will be easier for him to express himself in the absence of the accused, but those witnesses will be called. And I think that this is very useful in the determination of the truth. So we do not intend, in accordance with Rule 71, to hear witnesses by videolink. Witnesses who are fact witnesses and who can seriously inculpate the accused. To go back to the judicial notice that you mentioned, we primarily have in mind the issue of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the relevant times. This has already been the subject of some debate and discussion and evidence that was heard in other cases before this Tribunal. However, this discussion has not completed, has not been completed to this date. So we suggest that the Chamber base itself on the adjudicated facts in other cases as regards the issue of the armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the relevant times. For the time being, I see it as the only issue that we intend to invoke, in accordance with Rule 94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Terrier. That's very helpful for you to focus us on that. And I might get an initial reaction from the two Defence counsel on that, whether or not you think, after discussions, you may be in a position to agree to using judicial notice on adjudicated facts, just on that single issue on the nature of the armed conflict here, which I know you consider to be an issue in the case from your prior pleadings. You certainly don't have to give any final answer today. Mr. Terrier has put us on notice that that's something which he thinks is certainly worthy of discussion and might become the subject of a motion which he would put before the Chamber. If you wish to share with us your initial reaction, it certainly doesn't have to be your final position on that, I'd be happy to hear you. It might be useful to him too. Do either counsel wish to say something on this? Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, the musings of the Prosecutor, I take them to be just that, the musings. You will have to excuse us. Mr. Seric and myself are rather new here, and we are just studying the precedents of all the cases that were tried before this Tribunal. And as far as we know, no facts have been concluded, no judgements are final, because no cases have been completed, the appeals are still pending. So we don't know what are those things that our learned colleague from the Prosecutor thinks has already been adjudicated, because in the view of the Defence, no Trial Chamber has yet proven or accepted, established, that the existence of an international armed conflict in Bosnia. So in our discussions, we will have to go case by case to see what has been accepted and to see whether the Defence can admit to that or accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think we've established that it's the subject of discussion. Perhaps we can go no further than that. Now, the next and last issue on methods that I want both sides to think about and discuss before the next Pre-Trial Conference has to do with a motion which has already been submitted by the Prosecution and has been under advisement by the Chamber, I think, for more than a month, maybe two months now, and that is a motion made under Rule 95 -- I'm sorry, 94 ter, dealing with so-called affidavit evidence. Now, the Prosecution's submission was that because it is not feasible for them in many cases to satisfy technically the requirement of an affidavit because Bosnian law doesn't recognise that particular term, and they think many of their witnesses would have some problem in testifying even before -- or in making out an affidavit or formal statement before the local judges, which has been done in some other cases, they would like the Chamber to interpret Rule 94 ter to allow a procedure whereby the Prosecutor's staff would take the statement and would require the witness to, in effect, affirm that they were telling the truth under pain of any penalty that would follow a false statement for the Tribunal. Now, we've heard from Mr. Krsnik about all -- I've read with great interest and care the oppositions that you have filed to that. The first thing I'd like to ascertain, however, is we have not heard from Mr. Martinovic's counsel, and I wondered if you wanted to say something on that issue here today. You received that motion, I take it, a few months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did receive the motion, and speaking conditionally, if the witness statements that the Court and the Prosecution and the Defence are of such probative value, then what is at issue is what the other indirect evidence -- what is the importance of that indirect evidence. The Rule, as is stands, is fine. So speaking conditionally, I cannot say whether I agree or not. I can say that on a case-by-case basis, depending on each individual witness statement. If the witness statement is good, then we do not need the indirect evidence, the indicia, the circumstantial evidence that would speak to the credibility of the witness statement that is at issue and that the Prosecution uses to prove a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to give Mr. Terrier a chance to add any additional thoughts he has on it. But I'm not going to -- this is a matter which would have to be ruled upon by the entire Chamber, obviously, and I'm not going to rule upon it today. But I will relay back to them the comments that are made. I wish to inform you of one thing, and that is that the Chamber has been seriously considering this. It has not been sitting on the table not being looked at, as it were. And one question which I would address to you is that Rule 94 talks about an affidavit or formal statement which is signed by a witness. This is in corroboration cases in accordance with the law on procedure for such state in which such affidavits or statements are signed. Now, in your motion, you told us about one provision in Bosnian law which allows evidence to come in if it is sworn before a local judge, I think. But a question that was raised in our mind is whether or not there is not some provision in Bosnian law which would be in full accord with the terms of 94 ter which do not require that the statement be sworn before a local judge, but rather that it be acknowledged before some authority that's recognised by Bosnian law akin to the kind of notary, or notary public which we have not only in French law but in American law, and in at least one of these cases in this Tribunal has been accepted under 94 ter. In other words, you don't have to have a local magistrate, but does Bosnian law recognise a kind of statement which is confirmed before a type of notary? In that regard, we plan to submit a letter to the Bosnian government simply asking them for information about the state of their law as to whether or not they have a kind of notary procedure but -- which again, I point out, has been accepted in other cases before this Tribunal. But I would like to find out from you whether or not, from your point of view, if such a system existed, that would alleviate some of the concerns you have or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, Mr. Stringer will answer your question on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam President, and greetings to counsel. Your Honour, in respect of this issue, your first question and the question of the Trial Chamber, in respect of whether provisions exist under Bosnian law for what we call a notary in the English language, I've had some dealings with this issue for some time now. It's my vague impression that there may exist in Bosnian law such a provision; however, it's not found in any of the laws or procedures that apply in criminal proceedings. It may be that such a person exists under the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina in other sorts of areas, other legal areas, such as areas involving real estate, other forms of property, other areas in which persons may be called upon to notarise or to place some sort of official seal or to ascertain the authenticity of signatures on documents. So it may be that a provision exists under some part of the law in Bosnia-Herzegovina; however, I don't believe it exists under the law that applies in criminal proceedings. The law that we've cited in the motion is what we believe is the closest provision that exists; that is, Article 230 which empowers a judge to put a witness under oath and to take a statement during the pre-trial or investigative phase of the case. But as Your Honour is aware, that procedure is only -- can only be used in Bosnia when there is an apprehension that the witness, because of sickness or some other reason, will not be able to appear at the hearing. So that is really something that's the opposite from what's envisioned in our Rule, and applying the language of 94 ter strictly, we don't think that we can meet that criterion in terms of illness or other reasons which would prevent a witness from coming to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Stringer, however, in reading the question, I don't propose to answer it, but the question is at least raised by the wording of 94 ter, whether or not the procedure which is talked about in accordance with the law and procedure in which such affidavits or statements are signed relates to the fact that it is legal to have a particular official witness the statement, as opposed to whether or not that particular witness statement would be admissible in a criminal proceeding in that particular country. For instance, as I say, in at least one other proceeding, a statement that was notarised by an American notary public was accepted under this particular provision, whereas I think it would be probably doubtful whether or not that would be admissible in a criminal proceeding. This is simply a question that has been troubling us. I think it's no secret that the interpretation of 94 ter is involved in many cases before -- several cases before the Tribunal, and in fact we do have an interlocutory appeal which is pending upon whether or not a witness statement that was taken by a prosecutor, not perhaps under the exact wording of the oath that you -- not the oath, but the acknowledgement that you propose, whether or not that is admissible. So I simply wanted to apprise you of this. We are working on it, and we will come down with a ruling on that in time to make it of use to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, the next item, and I am bound to get us out of here within the next -- all right. Mr. Krsnik, do you have something to say? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but I do believe an intervention is in order. Madam President, my colleague and myself, and most of us, the Defence counsel representing our clients here before this Court, we graduated from law schools in the former Yugoslavia. I just want to present a view that is contrary to the one expressed by my learned colleague. I think that he is not really familiar with what he terms "the Bosnian law." This law has not changed substantially from the law that was in effect in the former Yugoslavia, the criminal and property law. In fact, there was substantial law and procedural law in Yugoslavia and all of the republics. It is similar to the system that is in effect in the United States. For some -- in some cases, some cases are tried under the federal law and some under the republican law. After all the events that we are familiar with, these laws have changed to a very little degree. What I want to say is that in the criminal procedure law in force both in Bosnia and in Croatia, it does not envisage the possibility of oath-taking similar to the one that is in effect here. The witness is presumed to be under an obligation to speak the truth. They do not take an oath. It is presumed that they are speaking the truth. And if it is proven that they haven't been speaking the truth, then appropriate measures are taken. And as to notaries public, this system of notaries public has not been established in Bosnia-Herzegovina yet. In Croatia there is such a system in place. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, all the statements and all the other papers that need to be notarised, in France, in the US, and so on, they have to go to the local authorities, to the municipal administrative body, and have it notarised there. So what is being discussed in Rule 94 ter, and what our learned colleagues from the Prosecution are talking about, it's irrelevant. And it is inappropriate, in fact, to use such statements taken in this way before this Court. This is a very short representation of the situation now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just make one very brief rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We were actually looking forward to getting the views of the Defence on this very point because I think it's clear to all of us that they are in a better position to know what is the law of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina now. In the response that was filed by counsel for Mr. Naletilic, there is no indication whatsoever of any disagreement with the characterisation of the law that the Prosecutor included in her submissions on this, including the copies of the legislation which we believe applies. And, of course, on the part of counsel for Mr. Martinovic, there was no response whatsoever. So it is, I think, something to be borne in mind at this late date the positions of counsel on what is the applicable law. That is number one. Secondly, it may be that counsel's in a good position to know the law that prevailed in the former Yugoslavia prior to its dissolution. However, the law that we've cited to the Trial Chamber is the current law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, their laws on criminal procedure enacted in December of 1998. So again, we believe that's the current law. It's certainly law that was enacted in that country long after the former Yugoslavia ceased to exist, and it is the law which, in our view, comes closest to what is envisioned by Rule 94 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. This particular debate will be continued inside Chambers, and we'll will let you know how we come out of that. But I point out to you that I take no umbrage at all with your statement of the law in Bosnia insofar as 230 is concerned, and as far as the criminal procedure goes. The question that concerns the Chamber, because it is a Tribunal-wide question which has occurred in other cases too and is currently being debated in other cases, is whether or not if, indeed, the Bosnian law, under your view, would allow only something in its present form, pursuant to 230, whether or not we should then take the step ahead that you urge upon us and the Defence counsel would be very negative about. So we're seeking to look at all possible alternatives before we make that choice. Now, let me talk a little bit about the next step before the Pre-trial Conference, which in light of some of the information that we have gotten so far suggests that that will probably be in early July, by which many of these other disclosure requirements should be satisfied. Now, I point out to you that what I'm aiming at, what I am aiming at and I hope you all are aiming at, is that we would be through with the pre-trial stage of the case in -- certainly by the end of September. In other words, the case would be ready, positioned, to go to trial by the end of September. Now, I know you might say, "A-ha, but what are the possibilities that we really would be able to go to trial?" As you know, our Chamber is currently occupied with two trials; one of them, with any kind of luck, will be over, the trial phase will be over in the late fall; the other one we're not sure about, but we're aiming about something that's close to that. There, too, is also the possibility that another Chamber might become free and be able to take the case if it were positioned. So I think there is a real virtue in us having all the pre-trial management phase done by the end of September. And as I say, I would envision having another Pre-Trial Conference in early July. Now, let me -- that would also assure Mr. Naletilic's 120-day right to be heard from from the time of his Initial Appearance. But let me tell you what I hope the parties will be able to do aside from the disclosure business that we talked about earlier. One, I think that the parties should get together and exchange information and documents to the point that they can decide and tell me at the next Pre-Trial Conference what points are disputed and what are undisputed in the indictment, almost paragraph by paragraph, to see whether indeed there are some things which it is not necessary for you to dispute in order to provide the fullest possible defence to your clients. So we're hopeful that you would be able to come to us, as has been done in some of the other cases of which I'm familiar with it, the indictment which says, "Paragraphs 1, 2, and 3," or "Parts of paragraphs 1, 2, and 3 we don't dispute; the rest we do." That would be helpful. Rule 65 ter (E) requires that the Prosecutor go first in terms of putting together some statement for the Chambers of exactly what the issues will be in the trial. And Rule 65 ter (E) requires that that pre-trial brief, which I would see as coming sometime in September so that we can have a final Pre-Trial Conference at the end of September, that that would include, as is in the Rule, a preliminary statement on the facts and the law from the Prosecutor's point of view; a statement on the points of law and fact that are disputed and undisputed; and a list of witnesses, I'm now talking mainly from the Rule, with any requests for pseudonyms, and the estimated time that their testimony will take. Let me make three comments vis-à-vis witnesses: One, the Chamber would really like to know, and hopes the Prosecution will be in a position at that time to know what protective measures, such as facial distortion, pseudonyms, keeping the name out of the public domain, even in extreme cases -- and I point out very extreme cases -- closed session that the Prosecution will be requested for witnesses ahead of time. In some other trials, as I'm sure you're aware, it's caused some delay in the trials to have those arise at the last minute. Now, the Rule also requires that the Prosecutor include a summary of the witness' testimony. I've seen various forms of summaries. Some of them appear to be merely a kind of summary of the statement as the statement which is not too helpful for us. I think that the summary should be very specific as to the points of the indictment or the Prosecution's theory of the case that are affected or that are made -- that the witness' statement is relevant to, because that will make it much easier to move ahead. I hope this does not fall on deaf ears, but we must emphasise the need for, in all cases possible, shortening the list of witnesses, and perhaps classifying them in terms of the importance and again, whether their evidence might be taken by deposition or by affidavit because I'm sure you're all aware of the number of cases that are waiting to be tried and it will take an interminably long time if every single case has hundreds of witnesses and takes more than a year to try. It simply will be impossible to get the work of the Tribunal accomplished. So with that in mind, I would like to hear, even now, very preliminarily, and I think you can give this to me because it would be a very preliminary estimate, of the number of witnesses you think -- the range of the number of witnesses that you think that you'll be calling. And I'm going to ask the Defence witnesses the same. Knowing that you can't tell finally until, perhaps, a few months from now. But give me a rough idea of how many witnesses you think you're going to be calling, live witnesses, at this stage. Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, as you say, today it is very difficult to be precise in response to your question. So what I can tell you at this point, and I have to express myself under a caveat because we do not know what is going to be accepted as a fact not in dispute to this date; and secondly, we still do not know whether we will be able to use the procedure provided for by Rule 71 or Rule 94 bis. So with this double caveat, we can tell you that we intend to call to testify before the Tribunal, before the Chamber sitting in full, between 60 and 70 witnesses. If we count one witness per day, we will be able to hear -- we would actually be able to hear 1.5 witnesses per day, working day, and this applies only to the Prosecution's time. So that will take us to 45 to 47 days of hearing, and this is indeed a very rough estimate that I'm able to give you today. We hope that we will be able to further reduce the number of witnesses. Thank you, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You've told us that at the present time the range would be in the vicinity of nine weeks; right? Forty-five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I understand the Defence's job of estimating is a much more difficult one at so early a stage in the game, but perhaps you can give us a notion of the range of numbers of witnesses that you think you may bring in for the Defence. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Madam President, you are indeed right. The position of the Defence right now, and I believe for the entirety of the trial, will be more difficult because we do have a feeling that our learned colleagues from the Prosecution are more privileged than we are. I don't have my team as yet. I did not receive a decree nominating my co-counsel, and only today did I receive the decision that I have been appointed for three months, provisionally. So I don't have the security, and all this results in a certain insecurity in the Defence counsel. For all these reasons, the Defence really, for the time being, cannot envisage the number of witnesses or the number of trial days for the Defence. And what we really depend on is the quality of the witness statements tendered by the Prosecution. Only then will we be able to give you an answer and to reply to those allegations with our witnesses. My client has been charged with 22 points of the indictment. I need, let's say, two witnesses for each count, and that would take us to 44 witnesses, let's say. So the roughest estimate would be the same number of trial days as my learned colleague. But do not take us -- do not hold us to that. This really is the roughest of estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No. This is not a committal, but it gives us some idea in planning. And I would expect by the time of the next Pre-Trial Conference, in early July, when you've received all of these witness statements, that you would give us a much firmer number. How about you, Mr. Seric? Remembering that there may well be that between you one witness may serve, in some cases, both of your purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, absolutely, and not only that. According to the preliminary discussions between myself and my colleague, we will have joint witnesses, so to speak, which will reduce the number of witnesses required for each individual Defence. Regardless of the fact that this is a joint indictment, the places and counts are different for each of the indictees. My position is a bit more favourable, since I did receive the provisional decision on appointment several months before my colleague, so I do not have any complaints, despite the fact that not all of my colleagues in the team have been paid, those working in the field. The Defence has contacted about 151 witnesses so far. We intend to call anything between 60 and 70 witnesses, similar to the number called by the Prosecution. Some of the witnesses may overlap with the Defence of Mr. Krsnik. I cannot tell you that with any certainty because I have not been able to advise Mr. Krsnik about the material that I received from the Prosecution because I was told to keep it confidential. So this is just a preliminary statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. I certainly hope that you and your -- the other Defence counsel can get together and eliminate any duplication in terms of your witnesses, as has been done in some other joint trials in the Tribunal, because otherwise we will go on for years and years and I don't intend that that should happen. I'd also remind the Defence that during this period when the Prosecution is working to put together, with an aim for September, its pre-trial -- final pre-trial brief, that very soon thereafter, under Rule 65 ter (E), the Defence must also come up with some brief of its own, talking about which facts it disputes and does not dispute, and also that under Rule 67(A), if either of your clients intends to offer any special defences, like alibi, mental incapacity, that they must be made as soon as possible. I'm well aware of Mr. Naletilic's ongoing examination, and I assume that whatever that produces, you will take that into regard. But if there are to be any defences such as mental incapacity, physical inability, alibi, that sort of thing, then they should be made as soon as you have the necessary information and facts. Also, at an early point, and certainly by the next Pre-Trial Conference, we would like to know whether the defendants themselves plan to testify or not. I have a few other things to talk to you about very briefly, about the so-called house rules and our Trial Chamber and the way this Trial Chamber handles trials, which will affect the kind of papers that you file. We do have a working practice in the Chamber that requires the parties, before you file any motion with the Chamber, that the parties, the Defence counsel and the Prosecution, should at least contact each other and talk with the other side, attempting to either reach an agreement or to narrow the areas of difference, rather than just sending us the paper motion and then we find out by the reply that there really isn't an issue or the issue is much narrower or it could have been worked out. So we want you to at least talk to each other before you file formal, written motions with us. If it is a relatively simple matter, we would prefer that you consider making an oral motion instead of a written one. Now, I understand when we're in the pre-trial period, we're not in trial every day. But if it is a motion which can, for instance, wait until the next Pre-Trial Conference and will not unduly inhibit your preparation for trial, then we would rather be able to take care of it then but not at the expense of delay. If you need to get it in and get it decided, then go ahead and file it. We do have a rule because this is a mixed Chamber, for which I'm responsible because I'm the English speaking member of it and my colleagues speak French more natively than I do, but we do have a rule for all of our cases now that written motions be filed in both French and English. And lastly, as you prepare your exhibits for trial, and part of the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief has to be a list of exhibits that the Prosecutor intends to offer and if he anticipates -- if she anticipates objections by the Defence to those, please consult with the Registry about the method that this Chamber has been using in its present two trials in organising the exhibits in a way which we think cuts down considerably on the waste of time in the court so that we're not running around with pieces of paper before everybody. We do have a system which we have worked out which seems to be working well in the Kvocka and Krstic trials which are currently in operation, which has a system of pre-numbering the exhibits and cutting down on the time in trial. And you can certainly go to the Registry, Mr. Dubuisson, and you can find out about that, and I'd like you to do that. I also, finally, remind you that at the -- in one of the decisions which has already been rendered on the indictment in the Martinovic challenge, we did ask the Prosecutor in that case to think in terms of trial preparation in terms of the larger offences. This was an answer to challenges about cumulative charging. In other words, the trial may be facilitated if one thinks, and I think Mr. Terrier at an earlier oral argument on this, you agreed with that, with Judge Rodrigues, that if you think in terms of preparing the case in terms of the greatest or the largest or the highest hierarchy offence, as it were, that that may facilitate -- because however we come out ultimately on the question of cumulative charging, many of the other offences, or large parts of them, will be consumed in the more serious offence. Now, that concludes basically the things that I wanted to cover in this conference. I have alerted you to the fact that we will have another conference in early July, and we will tell you about that, and I expect the disclosure to be finished and I expect to have firmer answers on many of the other questions which have been raised and which, when you get a copy of the transcript of this Status Conference, you will be able to see. We will hope to have an answer to your motion by that time to facilitate your preparation. At this point, I'd like to find out if either the Prosecution or the Defence has anything further they want to raise now, and then I will ask Mr. Martinovic, our accused, if he has anything he wishes to raise about the conditions of his detention. Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, I have a very brief question concerning the language or, rather, the languages of this Tribunal. We will prepare a pre-trial brief. I can no longer find the French term for it. We will compose it in English. But do we have to translate it into French at the same time, and do we have to file both versions at the same time? It's a technical problem that we are faced with, and I should like to hear the decision of the Court on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, it has been the newly-announced position of the Chamber that we do wish to have them filed simultaneously, because French and English are the working languages of the Tribunal, under the Rule and, I believe, also under the Statute. And because we do have both native-speaking French and native-speaking English Judges, we would like them to be filed simultaneously. Do I have any questions from the Defence? Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have three points that I wish to advise you about, Your Honour. First of all, I would like to inform this Chamber that about three weeks ago -- Mr. Terrier, when was it that we last had a discussion with you? I think it was three weeks ago. My client, Mr. Mladen Naletilic, who I feel -- everybody seems to be forgetting the fact that he is a seriously ill person. He is a heart patient, cardiac patient. He was in this Court. He was closed up in a separate room for four and a half hours, and of course he was ill and the nurses had to intervene. He got his medication. And I have been asking for an explanation of that incident and have yet to receive one. The second issue. My client is allegedly, according to the Rules, obliged to wear a bulletproof vest, which is very heavy. Your Honour, this bulletproof vest will kill him before saving his life, because with his fragile health condition, just imagine what it is like for him to be wearing this heavy bulletproof vest, which is almost 20 kilos. So I would like this Trial Chamber to issue an order for him not to be obliged to wear it, because it does more harm than good. And, finally, you received my motion in which I asked for an expert evaluation, and both to you and to the Registry, I supplied some names, and I had a reason to do so. We have a problem now. Of course, my client trusts the appointed doctors, but he does not want to relate to them before the doctors that he trusts, especially the psychologists from Croatia that he already was in touch with, because as you know, the trust is the most important thing in the patient-doctor and the patient-psychologist relationship. On the other hand, you ordered that this evaluation be completed by the 25th of May. It will not be possible to complete it by that time unless the attending physicians from Croatia, in particular, Dr. Cikaz [phoen] from the Revro [phoen] hospital in Zagreb, and Dr. Maja Stroci [phoen], who in fact performed three surgeries on my client's heart, they should help the team that is going to be doing the evaluation in order to speed this whole process up. So I would like to ask the Trial Chamber respectfully to meet those requests of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, enlighten me. Who obliges your client to wear the bulletproof vest? That's an obligation imposed by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I would suggest that -- first of all, we won't even have a Status Conference for another month and a half, but I would suggest that you be in touch with the Registry, who takes care of the logistics of getting both accused and witnesses to court, to find out where that obligation is coming from and to see if you can't work it out at that level. As for the expert evaluation, now, as I recall, we did accord with your wishes that -- at least I think one of the persons conducting the investigation was someone suggested by you. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And the Registry is the one who is accorded, under the law, with the responsibility of picking out the approved people to conduct it. But if my recollection is correct, at least one of the people that you suggested and wanted to was on that team. So I'm not entirely clear. Is it that you don't think that the team will meet the deadline, or what is it exactly that you're ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. Today is the 16th of May, and the evaluation should be completed by the 25th. And for a serious, good evaluation of my client, taking into account the condition -- his condition, it cannot be completed by the 25th, especially if the doctors see him for the first time and especially in light of the fact that they received the documents only yesterday. So in order to speed the whole process up, we should have Dr. Cikaz and Dr. Maja Stroci assist them, because only in that way will this evaluation be completed in time and in an appropriate fashion. Especially after this evaluation, after the findings and the opinion, the Prosecution may want to cross-examine the experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What I want to tell you is I wish you to get in touch with the Registry and the people who made the initial selections and are overseeing this examination to see if you can work out, in a consensual way, any of your time problems before you come back to the Chamber. As you know, it's an important examination, but until we know what the results are, it's very difficult not only for you to proceed but even for the rest of us to get on with our work and to see whether or not this, in fact, will be a joint trial. So there is a premium on getting it done. Now, initially that date was set, and I don't remember the date of the order, but I don't remember that anybody objected at that moment and said, "We can't meet that deadline." So I would suggest that you talk with the relevant people in the Registry to register any suggestions you have for speeding this up before you -- certainly before the Chamber takes any action on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is familiar with that. I just wanted to advise the Chamber about those things that are ongoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will get in touch with the Registry, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, Mr. Krsnik has just said that the Prosecution should cross-examine those expert witnesses. I'm somewhat surprised --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but even maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm still surprised, because I did not think that this would present a defence by the accused. I thought that it was only a matter of health care involving the current situation of Mr. Naletilic and the need to provide the medical services in the best possible way. If this is, indeed, the case, we are in favour of everything that can be done in order to ensure Mr. Naletilic excellent treatment for his condition. However, if we are dealing with Rule 94 bis, if we are dealing with an expert report that is going to be communicated to the Prosecutor and the Chamber, this is an altogether -- this is a completely different problem. This now presents a type of defence offered by the accused. If that is the case, we have to be made familiar exactly with the type of defence he intends to offer, whether we are talking about his diminished responsibility or lack of his responsibility at the relevant times. And, secondly, if this is still a defence offered by the accused, we wish to be able to also have a say in the appointment of experts. But of course we think that the issue goes, first of all, to the health care that has to be provided to Mr. Naletilic while he's in the detention unit, and that particular health care has to be the best possible he can get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, let me just read a line from the Chamber's order of 18 April, which says: "Noting the oral motion of the Defence in which the accused asks for an examination to evaluate his mental and physical capacity to attend and participate in trial proceedings, noting that the Prosecution indicated it did not oppose the oral Defence motion for such examination at the Initial Appearance, noting that 74 bis permits the Trial Chamber to order it, for the foregoing reasons orders that an expert medical and psychological evaluation of the accused Mladen Naletilic be conducted to determine his mental and physical capacity to attend and participate in his trial." Now, I think that that's fairly clear, what the purpose is. I think it would be premature at this point for us to -- certainly, until they get that report, I don't see how they can possibly decide whether or not they are going to try to present any kind of motion along these lines. So I would suggest if they can get together with the Registry, get this report in. Then we will know where we're at, and any appropriate motions can be made from that time on. If there isn't anything else, I would like to call upon the accused, who has been very patient here, Mr. Martinovic, and ask him if he has any concerns about conditions in detention that he would like to raise with us at this time. Mr. Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have any complaints about the detention. I have complaints about the Defence, because the team has not been established yet and we are not able to work on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I have your concern under appraisal, Mr. Martinovic, and your Defence counsel has already articulated the concern, and we hope that -- he is your Defence counsel now. He is fully authorised to go ahead and continue with your defence, and we certainly hope that any of these problems we will try to work out with him so that you will be fully and fairly represented. Thank you. If there are no other concerns, then we will adjourn this Pre-Trial Conference. We all have to be very busy in the ensuing several weeks. There are motions which have to be outgoing, which have to be decided. We will get the report on one of the accused's condition. And we will be in touch with you as to the time of the next Pre-Trial Conference, and we sincerely hope that you will work on getting the answers to the questions we've talked about and hopefully cutting down on the number of issues which will be disputed, with -- perhaps this is too optimistic -- the hope that the number of witnesses that both sides plan to call can also be cut down. Thank you. This Status Conference is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: adjourned at 5.46 p.m.
